title: Article use
about: Greek uses the definite article far more than English: with names of people and places, with abstract and general nouns (*η ζωή*, *η μουσική*), with possessives (*το σπίτι μου*) and after demonstratives (*αυτό το βιβλίο*). It drops the indefinite article where English keeps it, above all for jobs and roles after *είμαι*.

items.en: Maria works in a bank.

errs.why: Names of people take the article in Greek: *η Μαρία*, *ο Νίκος*. You drop it only when you call someone (*Μαρία, έλα!*).

items.en: I really like music.

errs.why: General and abstract nouns take the definite article: *μου αρέσει η μουσική*, *η ζωή είναι ωραία*.

items.en: I'm a student at the University of Athens.

errs.why: Jobs and roles after *είμαι* or *γίνομαι* take no article: *είμαι φοιτητής*, *θέλω να γίνω γιατρός*.

items.en: Where's my mobile?

errs.why: Possessives come after a noun with the article: *το κινητό μου*, *η μητέρα σου*.

items.en: I want to read this book.

errs.why: After *αυτός* and *εκείνος* the article stays: *αυτό το βιβλίο*, *εκείνη η μέρα*.

items.en: We have lived in Athens for two years.

errs.why: Cities and countries take the article, so *σε* fuses with it: *στην Αθήνα*, *στο Λονδίνο*, *στην Ιταλία*.

items.en: I'm going home, I'm very tired.
items.why: Nothing to fix: *πάω σπίτι* "go home" is a set phrase without article or preposition (*πάω στο σπίτι* is also fine).

items.en: All the students passed the exams.

errs.why: *όλος* is followed by the article: *όλοι οι φοιτητές*, *όλη η μέρα*, *όλο το βράδυ*.

items.en: Mr Antoniou is waiting for you in his office.

errs.why: Talking about someone, titles take the article: *ο κύριος Αντωνίου*, *η κυρία Παππά*, *ο γιατρός Λαμπρόπουλος*. Without the article only when you address them: *Κύριε Αντωνίου!*

items.en: My father is an engineer at a big company.

errs.why: No indefinite article with a job after *είμαι*: *είναι μηχανικός*. *Ένας* is only added when an adjective describes the person: *είναι ένας πολύ καλός μηχανικός*.

items.en: I'm good at maths.

errs.why: School subjects and fields take the article: *τα μαθηματικά*, *η ιστορία*, so *στα μαθηματικά*.

items.en: I'll see you on Saturday.

errs.why: Days, months and seasons as time expressions are just article + accusative: *το Σάββατο*, *τον Αύγουστο*, *το καλοκαίρι*.

items.en: Health is the most important thing.

errs.why: Abstract nouns used in general statements take the article: *η υγεία*, *η ελευθερία*, *ο χρόνος*.

parts: Ο Νίκος έχει αυτοκίνητο, αλλά πηγαίνει στη δουλειά με τα πόδια.
items.en: Nikos has a car but walks to work.
items.why: Nothing to fix: after *έχω* Greek often leaves out *ένα* (*έχει αυτοκίνητο*, *έχεις παιδιά;*), and "on foot" is *με τα πόδια*.

items.en: Greece joined the EEC in 1981.

errs.why: Country names take the article as subjects too: *η Ελλάδα*, *η Γαλλία*, *ο Καναδάς*.

items.en: Patras is the third-largest city in Greece.

errs.why: Superlatives and ordinal numbers take the definite article: *η τρίτη μεγαλύτερη πόλη*, *ο πιο ψηλός*.

items.en: Man is a social being.

errs.why: A noun meaning a whole kind takes the definite article: *ο άνθρωπος*, *η γάτα είναι ζώο*, *οι γάτες κοιμούνται πολύ*.

items.en: Cats sleep many hours a day.

errs.why: General statements about a whole class use the article, singular or plural: *οι γάτες*, *η γάτα*. English drops it here; Greek does not.

items.en: In the summer we visited the Parthenon and the Acropolis Museum.

errs.why: Names of monuments, buildings and institutions take the article: *τον Παρθενώνα*, *το Μουσείο της Ακρόπολης*, *τη Βουλή*.

items.en: She works as a consultant at an insurance company.

errs.why: *ως* "as" (in a role) is followed by the bare noun: *ως σύμβουλος*, *ως δασκάλα*.

parts: Ο ποιητής Κωνσταντίνος Καβάφης γεννήθηκε στην Αλεξάνδρεια το 1863.
items.en: The poet Constantine Cavafy was born in Alexandria in 1863.
items.why: Nothing to fix: one article covers the title and the name (*ο ποιητής Κωνσταντίνος Καβάφης*), and years take *το*.

items.en: Learning foreign languages opens the mind.

errs.why: A *να* clause used as the subject at the start of a sentence takes the neuter article: *το να μαθαίνεις*. After the verb it can go without: *είναι ωραίο να μαθαίνεις*.

items.en: The fact that he didn't come to the wedding upset me a lot.

errs.why: An *ότι* clause standing as subject at the start of the sentence needs *το*: *το ότι δεν ήρθε…*.

items.en: The law in question was passed two years ago.

errs.why: *εν λόγω* "in question" sits between the article and the noun and needs the article: *ο εν λόγω νόμος*, *της εν λόγω απόφασης*.

items.en: The conference dealt with climate change and its consequences.

errs.why: Abstract topics take the article after a preposition as well: *με την κλιματική αλλαγή*, *για την ανεργία*. English "climate change" has no article; Greek needs it.

parts: Ως πρόεδρος της επιτροπής, οφείλω να σας ενημερώσω για τις εξελίξεις.
items.en: As chair of the committee, I must inform you of the developments.
items.why: Nothing to fix: *ως* + bare noun for a role (*ως πρόεδρος*), and *της επιτροπής* keeps its article.
